note: Descriptive profiles; each claim cites data/sources.json ids. membership_series: published figures only, nothing interpolated; high=null means 'at least'. Countries come from group_countries.json, crime lines from groups_business.json (or 'lines' where that file has no entry).

profiles.name: Sinaloa Cartel
profiles.aka: Cártel de Sinaloa; split into Chapitos and Mayiza factions
profiles.what: Mexico's oldest major trafficking organisation, now split into two warring factions.
more: Grew out of the Guadalajara-era networks and was long run as a federation of semi-autonomous bosses (Guzmán, Zambada and others).
Since September 2024 the Chapitos (sons of Joaquín Guzmán) and the Mayiza (Zambada loyalists) have fought each other in Sinaloa after Ismael Zambada was taken to the US.
US agencies name it a main supplier of fentanyl and other drugs to the US; revenue figures are not reliably known.

profiles.name: Jalisco New Generation Cartel
profiles.abbr: CJNG = Cártel de Jalisco Nueva Generación
profiles.what: Fast-expanding Mexican cartel, reported in most Mexican states.
profiles.founded: 2010–11, Jalisco (Mexico), from the remnants of the Milenio Cartel and Nacho Coronel's network
more: Began as an armed wing (‘Matazetas’) after Ignacio Coronel's death in 2010; led for years by Nemesio Oseguera, ‘El Mencho’.
Mexico's financial intelligence unit reported operations in 27 states in 2020; its main rival is the Sinaloa Cartel.
Leadership after El Mencho is contested in reporting.
profiles.series_note: Published estimates (2022 model-based 28,764; 2026 NCTC 15,000–20,000) use different methods, so they are not plotted as a trend.

profiles.name: Gulf Cartel
profiles.what: Historic Tamaulipas border cartel, now split into rival factions.
more: Juan García Ábrego built it in the 1980s by moving Cali Cartel cocaine across the border; Osiel Cárdenas later created the armed wing that became Los Zetas.
Today it is fragmented into factions (Escorpiones, Ciclones, Metros and others) that fight over border crossings, drugs, arms and migrant smuggling.
profiles.series_note: No numeric membership estimate found (US NCTC says only ‘thousands’).

profiles.name: Northeast Cartel
profiles.what: Zetas successor group based in Nuevo Laredo.
profiles.founded: Mid-2010s, Tamaulipas (Mexico), splinter of Los Zetas
more: Emerged as Los Zetas broke apart; controls key crossings around Nuevo Laredo.
Detailed independent reporting on its structure is limited.

profiles.name: La Nueva Familia Michoacana
profiles.what: Michoacán-rooted group now strongest in Guerrero, Mexico State and Michoacán.
profiles.founded: 2000s, Michoacán (Mexico); current form after La Familia's 2010–11 break-up
more: Successor to La Familia Michoacana, whose split also produced the Knights Templar.
Known for extortion of farmers and businesses alongside drug production; it fights CJNG in the region.

profiles.name: Juárez Cartel / La Línea
profiles.what: Chihuahua border cartel whose armed wing La Línea now carries the name.
more: Rose under Amado Carrillo Fuentes in the 1990s; weakened by its 2008–12 war with Sinaloa in Ciudad Juárez.
Membership and revenue are not reliably estimated.

profiles.name: Clan del Golfo
profiles.abbr: also EGC = Ejército Gaitanista de Colombia (self-name)
profiles.what: Colombia's largest armed criminal group, a successor to right-wing paramilitaries.
more: Formed from demobilised AUC paramilitaries; also known as the Urabeños or AGC.
Run as a franchise-like network that subcontracts local gangs; Colombian forces count it in more than 200 municipalities.
It controls major Caribbean cocaine departure points and is in on-off talks with the government.
profiles.series_note: Colombian security-force counts (armed members plus support networks). Other claims (e.g. 13,500–14,000) are not plotted.

profiles.name: National Liberation Army
profiles.what: Colombia's last major leftist guerrilla, heavily involved in illicit economies.
more: Founded by students and priests inspired by the Cuban revolution.
Operates on both sides of the Colombia–Venezuela border, taxing cocaine, mining and contraband; it has fought FARC dissidents in Catatumbo.
profiles.series_note: Colombian security-force counts (armed members plus support networks).

profiles.name: FARC dissidents
profiles.abbr: EMC = Estado Mayor Central; Segunda Marquetalia and other splinters
profiles.what: Factions of the former FARC guerrilla that rejected the 2016 peace deal.
more: Not one group: the EMC, its offshoots and the Segunda Marquetalia compete as well as cooperate.
Security forces counted 3,919 in Iván Mordisco's EMC and 2,802 in Calarcá's EMBF as of July 2025.
profiles.series_note: Faction counts change as groups split, so no consistent series.

profiles.name: Tren de Aragua
profiles.what: Venezuelan prison-born gang that spread with the Venezuelan migration.
more: The name comes from a construction union on an unfinished railway in Aragua; Héctor ‘Niño Guerrero’ Guerrero built the group from Tocorón prison.
Venezuela retook Tocorón in September 2023; cells abroad act with much autonomy.
Its size and US reach are disputed.

profiles.name: Los Choneros
profiles.what: Ecuador's oldest major gang, long dominant in prisons and coastal routes.
more: Named after founder Jorge Véliz, ‘El Chonero’; grew under ‘Rasquiña’, killed in 2020, then ‘Fito’, who escaped prison in January 2024.
Ecuadorian police link its alliance to the Sinaloa Cartel.
profiles.series_note: US (12,000) and Ecuadorian government (30,000) figures conflict and count different things.

profiles.name: Los Lobos
profiles.what: Ecuador's largest gang by most estimates, a Choneros splinter.
profiles.founded: About 2019, Cuenca (Ecuador), from a Choneros cell
more: Led a breakaway coalition (‘Nueva Generación’) against the Choneros after Rasquiña's 2020 killing.
Ecuadorian police tie it to CJNG; it is also linked to illegal gold mining.
profiles.series_note: US (8,000) and Ecuadorian government (50,000) figures conflict.

profiles.name: First Capital Command
profiles.what: Brazil's largest criminal faction, a prison gang turned transnational cocaine network.
more: Founded by eight inmates after the 1992 Carandiru massacre, presented as a prisoners' ‘union’; led for decades by Marcos Camacho, ‘Marcola’.
Controls cocaine routes through Paraguay and Brazilian ports to Europe and Africa; rival of Comando Vermelho.
São Paulo operations have targeted PCC money-laundering schemes and fuel adulteration.
profiles.series_note: São Paulo prosecutors' figures as reported by G1; only two points.

profiles.name: Red Command
profiles.what: Rio de Janeiro faction, Brazil's oldest, expanding into the Amazon.
profiles.founded: Late 1970s, Ilha Grande prison, Rio de Janeiro (Brazil)
more: Formed in a prison where common prisoners mixed with political prisoners.
Main PCC rival; controls favelas in Rio and Amazon river routes.

profiles.name: Mara Salvatrucha
profiles.what: Street gang born in Los Angeles, rooted in El Salvador, Honduras and Guatemala.
more: In 2022 El Salvador's government cited about 70,000 gang members on the streets (all gangs); UK officials summarise MS-13 at about 78,000 members before the crackdown.
Since the March 2022 state of exception more than 84,000 people have been detained; by late 2023 over 52,000 alleged MS-13 members were in custody.
It remains active in Honduras, Guatemala and US cities; main rival is Barrio 18.
profiles.series_note: Pre-2022 estimates count members; post-2022 figures count detentions, so they are not plotted together.

profiles.name: Barrio 18
profiles.abbr: also 18th Street gang; Sureños and Revolucionarios factions
profiles.what: Los Angeles–born street gang, MS-13's main rival in Central America.
more: Split in El Salvador in 2005 into Sureños and Revolucionarios.
Strong in Guatemala and Honduras; heavily hit by El Salvador's state of exception.

profiles.name: Viv Ansanm / Gran Grif
profiles.what: Coalitions of armed gangs controlling most of Port-au-Prince and parts of Artibonite.
more: Viv Ansanm joined the previously rival G9 and G-Pèp alliances in 2024; Gran Grif operates in Artibonite.
